title: A Peek Inside the Pompeii of Greece
gist: Akrotiri, the Bronze Age Minoan city on Santorini preserved by a massive 16th-century B.C. volcanic eruption, was excavated starting in 1967 and fully uncovered by August 1969. The article is a short, paywall-truncated news brief with no further analytical content.

insights.claim: Akrotiri, a Bronze Age Minoan city on the volcanic island of Santorini in the southern Aegean, was fully uncovered by archaeologists on August 19, 1969, after excavations began in 1967.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Establishes a dated archaeological milestone; relevant for cultural-heritage/tourism context around Santorini but has no direct market signal.
insights.quote: on Aug. 19, 1969, the city was uncovered in its entirety—frozen in time, as Pompeii would be thousands of years later, by a thick coating of pumice and ash
insights.locator: opening paragraph, 'Even for a country with a past...'

insights.claim: Archaeologists believe the eruption that buried Akrotiri occurred sometime in the 16th century B.C. and was one of the largest volcanic eruptions in history, devastating multiple Minoan settlements.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: No exact date exists for the eruption, underscoring that ancient volcanic chronology remains uncertain even for one of history's largest eruptions.
insights.quote: we know it was one of the largest volcanic eruptions in history—devastating many settlements of the Minoan civilization, including Akrotiri
insights.locator: second paragraph, 'That pumice and ash came from...'

insights.claim: Akrotiri sits roughly 120 miles southeast of the Greek mainland, in the southern Aegean Sea.
insights.speaker: David Nield
insights.so_what: Basic geographic anchor for the site; minor factual reference only.
